title: Big Workers, Tiny Workers
text: How was this made? In 1565 Pieter Bruegel painted The Harvesters with oil paint on an oak board. It shows farm workers cutting and gathering wheat on a hot summer day. Kiddo, look at the workers up close and then at the people working in the fields behind them. Their sizes are very different. Look for little stories too, like a man asleep under a tree and a group eating lunch.
question: In The Harvesters, who is painted bigger: the workers in front or the people far back in the fields?
hints: Find the man asleep under the tree. Now look for the tiny dots out in the fields. Which group would you have to squint to see?
answer: the tiny ones way out in the fields

title: Small Means Far
text: Bruegel had to make a flat wooden board look deep. The tiny people at the back of the painting are not really tiny. Something far from our eyes takes up a smaller part of what we can see, so it looks smaller, just like a friend walking away from you. Bruegel paints things smaller the farther they are meant to be. That is how a flat painting can look as if you could walk into it.
question: A person near the back of the painting looks tiny. Are they really a tiny person?
hints: Picture a friend running to the end of a long street. What happens to how big they look to you?

title: Air Makes Pale and Blue
text: Bruegel used a second trick as well. Air is full of tiny bits of water and dust that scatter light. The more air between your eye and something, the paler and bluer it looks. Painters call this aerial perspective, while making faraway things smaller is called linear perspective. That is why the hills and the bay at the back of The Harvesters are pale and bluish and almost fade into the sky.
question: Why do the hills and the sea at the back of the painting look pale and bluish?
hints: Think of a hill seen on a long car trip and a tree right beside the road. Which looks sharper and darker?

title: Watching the Steps
text: Kiddo, people who study volcanoes watch for signs that something huge is on its way. On Elephantine Island, people in Egypt watched for a sign too. A stone nilometer had steps leading down into the Nile, and each summer day the water covered more of them. Everyone noticed, and everyone knew the flood was coming. The river spilled over its banks and spread across the fields, and after some weeks the water went down again. Imagine standing on those steps and watching.
question: If the water covers more and more of the nilometer steps each day, what is the river doing?
hints: Imagine you are standing on a dry step. What would have to happen to the water before it reached your feet?
answer: the water would have to get to my feet

title: Rain You Never Saw
text: Imagine you are a farmer beside the Nile. Hardly any rain falls on Egypt, yet your river swells every summer. The water comes from heavy monsoon rains on the Ethiopian highlands, far to the south. It rushes into the Nile and travels north. It carries dark mud washed off the mountains. When the flood spreads over the fields and slowly goes down, that mud, called silt, settles and makes the soil rich for the farmers' crops.
question: Egypt gets almost no rain, so where did the flood water come from?
hints: A river carries water from where it begins to where it ends. Where might this water have started its journey?
answer: at the beginning of the river i guess

title: A Year Built Around a Flood
text: The flood reached Egypt around July to September. The Egyptian year was built around it, with three seasons: Akhet (flood), Peret (growing) and Shemu (harvest). Officials measured each year's flood on stone gauges called nilometers, like the one on Elephantine Island. The height told them what harvest to expect. A flood that was too low left fields dry and could mean hunger, and one that was too high could wash away houses and dikes.
question: Why did officials want to know how high the flood rose each year?
accept: to know if there'd be enough food
hints: Picture a year when the flood was very low. What would be different for the families later in the year?

title: A Beat for Your Feet
text: Kiddo, can you find every step hiding in a march? The Stars and Stripes Forever by John Philip Sousa is a march, and its beat is steady and goes in twos, like walking feet. Stand up while it plays and step one foot on each beat. Listen for the steps as you go.
question: While the march plays, which two feet does the beat take turns with?
accept: both feet, one then the other
hints: Try walking across the room. What do your feet do, one after the other?
answer: they move forward and stomp on the floor

title: Why the Beat Stays Steady
text: Here is the next piece to collect: a clue about why a march never speeds up or slows down. A march keeps the same speed from start to finish so a band can play it while walking together. If the beat changed, the players' steps would stop matching, and they would bump into each other or fall out of line. Each player has to notice the others and stay with the beat. The beat works like a shared clock, and every foot lands on it at the same moment.
question: Why does a march keep the same speed the whole way through?
accept: so they can march and play
so nobody bumps into each other
hints: Think about what a band is doing with its legs while it plays.

title: The Piccolo's Second Tune
text: Can you find a tune hiding above the other tune? Near the end of the march, the piccolo plays its own whistling tune. The piccolo is the smallest and highest flute, and it plays high over the rest of the band. A second tune played over the main one at the same time is called a countermelody. The low brass instruments answer it, so high and low sounds take turns over the steady marching beat.
question: When the piccolo plays its own tune while the band plays the main tune, how many tunes are playing at once?
hints: Listen for the main tune the band plays. Is the piccolo playing that very same tune?

title: What's Under the Silence?
text: What's down there, underneath the quiet at the end of the story? A real wolf finally comes, and the boy shouts "Wolf!" again, but this time nobody comes. The two false alarms had taught the villagers that his shouts did not mean a wolf was there. His earlier lies made his true words sound like just another trick.
question: When the real wolf came, why didn't the villagers come to help?
accept: they thought it was a trick
hints: Think back to the first two shouts. What had the villagers found out about the boy's shouts?
If a friend's warnings had turned out empty twice, how would you feel about the third one?

title: What's Under the Words?
text: What's down there, underneath words that turn out to be wrong? What makes something a lie is what the speaker knows and means, not just whether the words turn out wrong. A mistake is fixed by finding out the truth. A lie costs trust, because people learn they cannot rely on that speaker.
question: Sam says "It's raining!" because he really thinks it is, but it isn't. Is that a lie or a mistake?
hints: What did Sam think was true at the moment he spoke?

title: The Farmer and the Snow
text: Here's something funny: Wilson Bentley, a Vermont farmer, pointed a microscope at snowflakes and photographed them. Every flake in his pictures looks different from the others. But there's a joke hiding in them, because they all have the same number of arms. Kiddo, take a close look at the photographs. Can you find the number?
question: Look at the snowflake photographs. How many arms does each snowflake have?
hints: Pick one arm and put your finger on it. Then go around the flake in order. How will you know when you're back where you started?
answer: when i get to the first arm again

title: The Square Snowflake Joke
text: A snowflake is made of ice, and ice is made of tiny bits of water too small to see. When water freezes, those bits fit together in six-sided rings. The rings join into a six-sided shape like a hexagon, and the arms grow out from its corners. So the ring's six sides become the flake's six arms. Now let's imagine something silly: a snowflake built from a different kind of ring.
question: Suppose the tiny bits of water fit together in four-sided rings instead of six-sided ones. How many arms would you expect a snowflake to grow?
hints: In a real snowflake, what do the sides of the ring turn into?

title: The Snowflake That Never Notices
text: Ice grows in a six-sided pattern, so a snowflake has six-fold symmetry. Turn it a sixth of a full turn and it looks exactly the same as before. It's like a prankster that keeps swapping places and says, "Nothing changed!" The arms match because all six grow at the same moment in the same air, so whatever shapes one arm shapes the others too. Fold a paper circle into sixths and cut it, and one snip makes the same shape in all six parts.
question: You turn a snowflake a sixth of a turn at a time. How many times does it look the same as it goes all the way around once?
hints: Picture a pizza cut into slices that are each one of those turns. How many slices make the whole pizza?
Does the very last turn bring the flake back to where it began? Think about whether that one counts.
answer: yes it goes back to the start

question: In The Harvesters, who is painted bigger: the workers in front or the people far back in the fields?

question: Egypt gets almost no rain, so where did the flood water come from?

title: What's Down Under the Shout?
text: What's down there, under a very old story? Let's dig in. In a fable credited to Aesop, a shepherd boy watches the sheep and shouts "Wolf!" just for fun. The villagers run to guard the sheep. But there is no wolf, and the boy does it again. This picture was made long after Aesop's time.
question: Why did the villagers run to the shepherd boy when he shouted "Wolf!"?
hints: What did the villagers notice when they heard the shout?

title: A Lie or a Mistake?
text: Here is something hiding down deeper. What makes something a lie is what the speaker knows and means, not just whether the words turn out wrong. A person who says something they believe, and it turns out wrong, is in a different spot from a person who says it knowing it isn't true. One kind is fixed by finding out the truth. The other costs trust, because people learn they cannot rely on that speaker.
question: Sam says "It's raining!" because he really thinks it is, but it isn't. Is that a lie or a mistake?
hints: What does Sam believe when he says it?

title: The Spinning Trick
text: What's funny about this? Spin a snowflake a little and it looks like nothing happened! Turn it one sixth of a full turn and it looks exactly the same. All the arms grow at the same moment in the same air, so what shapes one arm shapes them all. Fold a paper circle into sixths and cut it, and one cut makes the same shape in every part.
question: You turn a snowflake a sixth of a turn at a time. How many times does it look the same as it goes all the way around once?
hints: Picture a dot on one arm. After your first turn, where is the dot?
